title: Breaking and Fixing Defenses Against Control-Flow Hijacking in Multi-Agent Systems

object.carrier: Task-specific control-flow graph encoded as a context-free grammar over agent-call tokens (compiled to a parser with Lark) plus at most three natural-language contextual rules per CFG edge; generated by an LLM at planning time and enforced by an LLM judge inside the MAS orchestrator for the duration of the rollout

safety_property.statement: Every agent-to-agent invocation must correspond to an edge of a pre-generated permitted control-flow graph and satisfy that edge's contextual rules (input validation, contextual appropriateness, data provenance), so untrusted content cannot re-route orchestration toward unsafe agents/actions (arbitrary code execution via reverse shell; exfiltration by cc:-ing untrusted addresses or emailing internal-only data). The property fails when an attack reaches its adversarial objective (ASR > 0) or when sensitive data flows to unauthorized recipients even without an adversary (accidental violations).
safety_property.operationalized_as: ASR = percentage of attacks that reach the adversarial objective (open a reverse shell in coding tasks; add cc: to external untrusted 'support' address in computer-use tasks) over 3 trials per user task on CFH-Hard (Tables 1-3); benign task success rate (single-answer accuracy; open-ended graded by o4 LLM judge head-to-head wins+ties, Table 4) measures functionality cost; accidental-violation rate on vaguely worded non-adversarial inputs (Table 3 'Acc.' column, §6.6).

capabilities: Controls a single piece of untrusted content (Web page, document, email attachment, message, image) that a benign agent ingests - indirect prompt injection; does not control user prompts (unlike jailbreaking)

Phrases malicious instructions as fake error messages with step-by-step 'fixes' naming which agents to invoke and when; the orchestrator receives them via an inter-agent message from a trusted agent (confused-deputy control-flow hijacking)
Objectives: arbitrary code execution (reverse shell) in coding tasks; exfiltration by adding an external untrusted address to cc: of the system's next email in computer-use tasks
Attacker access escalates to agents' access: credentials, emails, calendars, files, logs, logged-in web views, containerized environments
assumptions: Users and all agents are benign; some agents ingest untrusted external content

Defense has access only to the orchestration layer (who talks to whom, when, about what); agents are black-box commercial LLMs whose prompts, weights, and reasoning traces are not visible or controllable

Instantiated on AutoGen Magentic-One (orchestrator o4, sub-agents GPT-4o, plus a simulated emailing agent); results expected to transfer across configurations/LLMs/platforms since CFH transfers (Triedman et al., 2025)
not_covered: Malicious insiders, compromised agents, or attacker-controlled users
CFH attacks that comply with the statically generated CFG (CFI-style evasion under over-approximation) - stated open question
Defense failures from LLM mistakes when generating the graph or rules (Appendix B); accidental violations investigated only on a small computer-use scenario

intervention.name: ControlValve
intervention.description: Two stages. Planning (before any untrusted content is ingested): an LLM generates (1) a task-specific context-free grammar over agent-call tokens defining admissible control-flow traces (few-shot examples of parseable grammars, no attack examples), compiled with Lark, and (2) at most three zero-shot natural-language contextual rules per CFG edge enforcing input validation, contextual appropriateness, and data provenance. Execution: before each agent transition A->B the orchestrator checks that the transition is a permitted CFG edge and an LLM judge verifies the edge's contextual rules against the conversation trace (the judge is not asked to weigh justifications, unlike alignment checks); outcomes are permit / reject / re-plan (max three re-planning attempts), otherwise block and notify the user. Implemented as part of the orchestrator without modifying sub-agents.

controls.name: LlamaFirewall (LF) with Llama / 4o-mini / 4o / o4-mini alignment-check backends

results.claim: ControlValve blocks all evaluated conventional IPI attacks: 0% ASR across all 3 presentations (InjecAgent, Greshake, AgentDojo) x 3 payloads (original reverse shell, our reverse shell, our computer-use cc: attack), where undefended MAS reach up to 100% ASR in the computer-use scenario.
results.setting: AutoGen Magentic-One MAS (orchestrator o4, sub-agents GPT-4o, simulated emailing agent); CFH-Hard dataset; attacker controls one piece of untrusted content but not user prompts

denominator.how_counted: Table 1 caption: Each cell is computed over three trials each of either ten (coding) or six (computer use) user tasks.

results.claim: ControlValve blocks all evaluated coding CFH (reverse shell) attacks: 0% ASR across all 8 templates (Generic, Python, WordPress x original and CFH-Hard; File Not Found, Agent Not Found), vs. 83-100% ASR for the undefended MAS.
results.setting: AutoGen Magentic-One MAS (orchestrator o4, sub-agents GPT-4o, simulated emailing agent); CFH-Hard dataset; attacker controls one piece of untrusted content but not user prompts; CFH attacks disguised as errors and laundered through trusted agents

results.claim: ControlValve blocks all evaluated computer-use CFH attacks and accidental violations: 0% ASR across 5 CFH-Hard templates plus the Accidental (vaguely worded, non-adversarial) template, vs. 67-89% ASR undefended.
results.setting: AutoGen Magentic-One MAS (orchestrator o4, sub-agents GPT-4o, simulated emailing agent); CFH-Hard dataset; attacker controls one piece of untrusted content but not user prompts; CFH attacks disguised as errors and laundered through trusted agents; computer-use tasks exfiltrate by cc:-ing an external untrusted address

results.claim: Our CFH-Hard attacks evade LlamaFirewall's default (Llama-backed) alignment checks: ASR is 80% for coding and 67% for computer use, improving on the original CFH attacks by up to 12x for 8 of 12 attacks.
results.comparison: up to 12x vs original CFH; 67% computer use
results.setting: AutoGen Magentic-One MAS (orchestrator o4, sub-agents GPT-4o, simulated emailing agent); CFH-Hard dataset; attacker controls one piece of untrusted content but not user prompts; CFH attacks disguised as errors and laundered through trusted agents; LlamaFirewall alignment checks with default Llama backing LLM
results.quote: Our CFH attacks (Tables 2 and 3) are much more effective, with the attack success rate (ASR) improving by up to 12×\times for 8 out of 12 attacks. ASR against the default LlamaFirewall configuration is 80%80\% for coding attacks, 67%67\% for computer use attacks.

results.claim: Accidental security violations without any adversary: the baseline MAS emails INTERNAL-ONLY data to an external destination 56% of the time (with or without LlamaFirewall); ControlValve reduces this to 13%.
results.setting: Computer-use scenario; input document annotated (INTERNAL ONLY, DO NOT SHARE); no adversarial input - derailment caused by vagueness/hidden requirements
results.quote: The baseline MAS does this 56%56\% of the time, with or without LlamaFirewall. The rate for ControlValve-defended MAS is 13%13\%.

results.claim: ControlValve maintains or improves benign performance: single-answer accuracy 97% (coding) / 100% (computer use) vs. base 93% / 89%; LLM-judge head-to-head (wins+ties) 56% vs. 44% on open-ended coding, 89% vs. 89% on computer use.
results.setting: Benign CFH-Hard tasks (no attack); single-answer scored by accuracy, open-ended graded by o4 LLM judge head-to-head

denominator.how_counted: Tables 7/8 captions: Accuracy is reported over three trials for each question (two per use case). Coding: 5 use cases x 2 questions x 3 trials = 30; computer use: 3 x 2 x 3 = 18.

results.claim: Defense reliability (ablation): with a maximum of three retries, o4-mini generates parseable control-flow graphs 100% of the time (avg 1.1 retries); weaker models struggle (4o: 96%/87%, 4o-mini: 80%/80% parse rate).

limitations.statement: ControlValve is not a perfect defense: if the LLM makes a mistake creating the graph or the rules, the defense can fail (uncommon; see Appendix B).
limitations.quote: We believe that ControlValve is a significant advance over the defenses based on alignment checks or (only) the principle of least privilege, but it is not a perfect defense. While uncommon (see Appendix B), if the LLM makes a mistake creating the graph or the rules, the defense can fail.

limitations.statement: As in CFI, the generated graph may be too lax (over-approximation of legitimate executions) and could permit executions that should not happen; whether CFH-style evasion complying with the CFG is possible in MAS is an open question.
limitations.quote: As in CFI (Abadi et al., 2005), the graph may be too lax (i.e., an over-approximation of the legitimate executions) and thus potentially permit executions that should not happen.

limitations.statement: If the generated CFG is too restrictive it may limit MAS functionality by preventing adaptive invocation of new agents/tools on genuine errors (investigated in Appendix F).
limitations.quote: If the generated CFG is too restrictive, it may limit functionality of MAS by preventing agents from adaptively invoking new agents and tools when they encounter genuine errors and faults. We investigate this failure mode in Appendix F.

limitations.statement: Accidental (non-adversarial) security violations are only demonstrated on a small computer-use scenario; a full investigation is beyond the scope of the paper.
limitations.quote: Security violations are not always caused by adversarial instructions. A full investigation is beyond the scope of this paper but we use our computer use scenario to demonstrate that control flow can be derailed due to vagueness and hidden requirements rather than adversarial inputs.

limitations.statement: All experiments run on a single MAS configuration (AutoGen Magentic-One, o4 orchestrator + GPT-4o sub-agents) to reduce evaluation cost; transfer to other configurations is expected, not shown.
limitations.quote: To reduce evaluation cost, we perform our experiments on this configuration, but we expect that the results transfer to other configurations.

counterexamples.description: CFH attacks evade LlamaFirewall alignment checks with every backing LLM tested (Llama, o4-mini, 4o, 4o-mini) by (a) presenting unsafe actions as necessary to complete the user's task and (b) laundering them through trusted agents; fundamental conflict between safety and functionality
AgentDojo-presentation IPI satisfies LlamaFirewall's own definition of alignment ('related to' and 'likely to further' the goal) and succeeds 63% against LF(llama) in the computer-use scenario
